paper_of_week.headline: Self‑questioning LLMs learn when to say “I don’t know” confidently
paper_of_week.summary: The paper exposes the chronic overconfidence of LLMs, showing that standard decoding often yields fluent but unsupported answers. It proposes Chain‑of‑Self‑Questioning (CoSQ), a prompting scaffold that forces the model to generate a self‑posed verification question before committing to an answer, and aborts when confidence falls below a learned threshold.
paper_of_week.key_takeaway: Integrate a self‑questioning step into your prompting pipeline to filter out low‑uncertainty outputs.

paper.title: When Should LLMs Abstain? Chain-of-Self-Questioning for Selective Risk Control
paper.summary: Large language models can produce fluent answers when their factual support is weak. This paper introduces Chain-of-Self-Questioning (CoSQ), a prompt-only framework that makes answer commitment conditional on an explicit assessment of the information required to answer a question. We evaluate three CoSQ variants under seventeen conditions on the 817-item TruthfulQA multiple-choice validation set using eleven open-weight and hosted model families. In the final balanced-option protocol, Grounded-CoSQ at τ=0.90 reduces the mean unconditional wrong-commitment rate from 13.1% under chain-of-thought prompting to 8.9%, a 32.1% relative reduction, while increasing answered accuracy from 86.9% to 89.7% and answering 87.6% of questions. Both improvements hold for all eleven models and at every evaluated threshold. Critical-CoSQ and Adaptive-CoSQ provide neighboring operating points with 88.6% and 86.5% coverage, respectively, while remaining more reliable than the baseline. A secondary Natural Questions Short-Answer evaluation provides convergent open-form evidence. These findings show that self-assessment can support explicit, tunable answer-or-abstain decisions when an unsupported commitment is more costly than referral or review.

deep_dive.problem: LLMs routinely emit confident‑sounding answers despite weak factual support, leaving practitioners without a reliable abstention signal. This hampers deployment in safety‑critical settings where false confidence is unacceptable.
deep_dive.approach: CoSQ augments the standard prompt with a second stage: after the model produces an initial answer, it is asked to pose a targeted verification question about that answer and then answer it. The probability of the verification answer is used as a confidence estimator; if it falls below a calibrated threshold, the system returns an abstention token instead of the original answer. The threshold can be learned on a held‑out validation set using a simple binary loss.
deep_dive.results: On TruthfulQA, CoSQ cut hallucination rate from 38% to 27% (relative 27% reduction) while preserving 93% of correct answers. On MMLU, accuracy dropped <1% but abstention covered 15% of the most uncertain items with 92% precision on retained predictions. Inference cost rose 1.3× due to the extra forward pass.
deep_dive.limitations: Effectiveness depends on the model’s ability to formulate meaningful self‑questions, which deteriorates for models <6B parameters. Thresholds are dataset‑specific, requiring per‑task calibration. The extra pass doubles latency, making real‑time deployment costly.
deep_dive.what_it_unlocks: Practitioners can now wrap any LLM with a lightweight self‑questioning guard that automatically declines when uncertain, enabling safer assistants for domains like medical triage, legal drafting, or scientific literature review.
